summary: Tractate Yoma daf 82a covers: Mishna: children are not afflicted on YK but trained gradually before bar/bat mitzvah; Children in danger of death: we violate YK to save them; Mishna: pregnant woman smells food - feed her until she recovers; Pikuach nefesh (saving life) overrides all of Yom Kippur.

display.whats: Mishna: children are not afflicted on YK but trained gradually before bar/bat mitzvah
display.hint: The Mishna rules that minor children are not required to fast on Yom Kippur, but in the year before they reach majority, they are trained to fast for increasing portions of the day.
display.title: Training Children to Fast Before Bar Mitzvah

learning.ahaMoment: The Mishna encodes a developmental theory of religious education: obligations are introduced gradually so they are internalized before they become formally binding.
learning.memoryAnchor: Children near bar mitzvah age are trained to fast gradually: preparation is required, not optional.
learning.learnerQuestion: Are children required to fast on Yom Kippur, and how are they prepared for the obligation?
learning.coreTension: Between the general rule that minors are exempt from the full obligations of the day and the educational need to prepare children to take on those obligations at maturity.
learning.coreMove: The Mishna establishes a graduated approach: young children are not required to fast, but in the years approaching majority, they are trained incrementally - beginning with partial fasts - so that the full obligation at bar/bat mitzvah is not a sudden shock.

takeaway.text: Preparing children for adult religious obligations is itself a mitzvah obligation on parents; the Mishna's graduated fasting rule is a model for how the Torah transitions minors into full observance.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may assume children are simply exempt with no educational requirement; the Mishna's graduated approach makes preparation itself mandatory.

argumentFlow.label: Mishnah: children are not made to fast, but are trained
argumentFlow.speaker: Mishnah
argumentFlow.text: Children are not afflicted by withholding food on Yom Kippur, but one trains them a year or two before maturity with a partial fast of several hours, so they grow accustomed to the mitzvot.

argumentFlow.label: Rav Chisda: feeble versus healthy child
argumentFlow.speaker: Mishnah
argumentFlow.text: Why state both 'one year' and 'two years'? Rav Chisda answers they describe different children: a feeble child is trained one year before maturity, a healthy child two years before.

argumentFlow.label: Age schedules of Rav Huna, Rav Nachman, Rabbi Yochanan
argumentFlow.speaker: Mishnah
argumentFlow.text: Rav Huna: a healthy child trains at eight to nine, completes the fast rabbinically at ten to eleven, and by Torah law at twelve. Rav Nachman shifts each stage a year later for boys. Rabbi Yochanan holds there is no rabbinic completion obligation before maturity at all.

misconceptions.misconception: Children must fast on Yom Kippur once they are old enough to understand.
misconceptions.correction: Minors are never made to fast a full day; the obligation is only to train them with partial fasts in the year or two before they reach the age of mitzvot.

visualizableElements.item: Mishna: children are not afflicted on YK but train

quizSeeds.question: Why does the Mishnah mention both 'one year' and 'two years' of training?
quizSeeds.answer: Rav Chisda explains they refer to different children: a feeble child is trained one year before maturity, a healthy child two years before.

quizSeeds.question: How does Rabbi Yochanan differ from Rav Huna and Rav Nachman on training children to fast?
quizSeeds.answer: Rav Huna and Rav Nachman hold there is a rabbinic obligation to complete the fast a year or two before maturity; Rabbi Yochanan holds there is no such rabbinic completion obligation before maturity.

sugyot.finalRuling: Minor children are not required to fast on Yom Kippur but are trained beforehand for increasing portions of the day, and Rav Chisda resolves the apparent contradiction between training a year before maturity and training two years before by explaining they describe different children: a feeble child trains for one year, a healthy child for two.
prerequisiteKnowledge: Understanding of Yom Kippur halachic framework

display.whats: Testing the Mishnah's 'one year or two years' against three views on training children to fast
display.hint: The Mishnah says a feeble child trains one year and a healthy child two years before maturity - how does this fit Rav Huna and Rav Nachman's view that this is completing the rabbinic fast, how does Rabbi Yochanan (who denies any such obligation) read the same words, and what settles whether 'training' means delaying a meal or completing the whole fast?
display.title: Testing 'One Year or Two Years' Across Three Views on Training

learning.ahaMoment: 'Training' is not one practice but two: for a young child it means pushing back mealtime by an hour, for an older child nearing maturity it means completing the entire fast - the same word covers both, and untangling them is what saves Rav Huna and Rav Nachman's reading from Rabba bar Shmuel's baraita.
learning.memoryAnchor: One year (feeble) or two years (healthy) before maturity: for Rav Huna/Rav Nachman this is rabbinic completion of the fast; for Rabbi Yochanan (no completion obligation) it marks how much earlier training itself begins. Training splits in two: delay a young child's meal, or have an older child finish the whole fast.
learning.learnerQuestion: How does the Mishnah's 'one year or two years before maturity' fit three different views on training children to fast, and what are the two senses of 'training' itself?
learning.coreTension: Between a single Mishnaic phrase ('one year or two years') and three different accounts of what it obligates, complicated further by two different things 'training' itself could mean.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara tests 'one year or two years' against three views: for Rav Huna and Rav Nachman, who hold a child fully completes the fast one (feeble) or two (healthy) years before maturity by rabbinic law, the phrase fits directly. For Rabbi Yochanan, who denies any such completion obligation, the same phrase instead marks how much earlier training begins for a feeble versus a healthy child. A baraita from Rabba bar Shmuel then threatens Rav Huna and Rav Nachman's reading by using 'training' language for what looks like the same one/two-year distinction; they resolve it by distinguishing two senses of training - delaying a young child's mealtime by an hour, versus having an older child actually complete the fast.

takeaway.text: The word 'training' covers two distinct practices - delaying a young child's meal versus having an older child complete the whole fast - and keeping them apart is what lets the Mishnah's 'one year or two years' support three different halachic readings without contradiction.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may assume 'training a child to fast' is a single, uniform practice; the sugya turns on there being two genuinely different things called 'training' at different ages, which is exactly what lets Rav Huna and Rav Nachman answer Rabba bar Shmuel's baraita without abandoning their view.

argumentFlow.label: Applying the Mishnah's 'one or two years'
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara tests the Mishnah's 'one year or two years' against the three opinions. For Rav Huna and Rav Nachman it fits: a feeble child completes the fast the year before maturity, a healthy child two years before, by rabbinic law.

argumentFlow.label: Difficulty for Rabbi Yochanan
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: For Rabbi Yochanan, who denies any rabbinic completion obligation, what could 'one or two years' mean? He reads it as the single year before maturity, with the one-versus-two distinction tracking feeble versus healthy children, not two separate years of obligation.

argumentFlow.label: Rabba bar Shmuel's baraita and the reply
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rabba bar Shmuel's baraita says one trains a feeble child one year and a healthy child two years before maturity. This fits Rabbi Yochanan but challenges Rav Huna and Rav Nachman, who answer that the 'training' mentioned there refers to completing the fast.

argumentFlow.label: Is 'training' the same as 'completing'?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara objects that training means doing only part of a mitzva, while completing means the whole fast, citing a baraita defining training as pushing the child's mealtime an hour later. Rava bar Ulla resolves it: there are two kinds of training, delaying a young child's meal and accustoming an older child to finish the fast.

misconceptions.misconception: 'Training' a child for the fast always means a partial, several-hour fast.
misconceptions.correction: There are two forms of training: the early-stage one delays mealtimes, but the later-stage 'training' near maturity does mean having the child complete the whole fast.

visualizableElements.item: Rav Huna/Rav Nachman: completing the fast; Rabbi Yochanan: earlier training start; two senses of training reconciled

quizSeeds.question: How does Rabbi Yochanan read 'one year or two years' if he denies a rabbinic completion obligation?
quizSeeds.answer: He takes it as the single year before maturity, with 'one or two' distinguishing feeble children from healthy children rather than marking two separate obligated years.

quizSeeds.question: How does Rava bar Ulla reconcile 'training' meaning a partial fast with the claim that it means completing the fast?
quizSeeds.answer: There are two distinct forms of training: delaying a young child's mealtime by an hour, and accustoming an older child to complete the entire fast.

sugyot.finalRuling: The Mishnah's 'one year or two years before maturity' is reconciled across three views: for Rav Huna and Rav Nachman it marks the rabbinic obligation to complete the fast, for Rabbi Yochanan it marks how much earlier training begins; and 'training' itself denotes two distinct practices - delaying a young child's mealtime, and having an older child complete the fast.

display.whats: Mishna: pregnant woman smells food - feed her until she recovers
display.hint: The Mishna addresses a pregnant woman who smells food on Yom Kippur and becomes unwell: she is fed until she recovers, even though it is Yom Kippur.
display.title: The Pregnant Woman Who Smelled Food

learning.ahaMoment: The Mishna encodes early intervention as a principle: we do not wait for a crisis to become obvious before acting to preserve life.
learning.memoryAnchor: Pregnant woman smells food and is distressed - feed her: don't wait for the crisis to escalate.
learning.learnerQuestion: What does the Mishna rule when a pregnant woman smells food on Yom Kippur and becomes distressed?
learning.coreTension: Between the YK eating prohibition and the obligation to protect the life of both the mother and the fetus.
learning.coreMove: The Mishna rules: if a pregnant woman smells food and becomes physically distressed, we feed her until she recovers, even on YK. We do not wait to see how serious the situation becomes - we act on the first sign of danger. The life before us is the priority.

takeaway.text: When a pregnant woman's physical state suggests danger from deprivation of food on YK, we feed her immediately without waiting to gauge severity; the precautionary application of pikuach nefesh is itself the ruling.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may expect a threshold of actual danger before the override kicks in; the Mishna rules that early signs of distress are sufficient.

argumentFlow.label: Mishnah: feed a craving pregnant woman and the ill
argumentFlow.speaker: Mishnah
argumentFlow.text: A pregnant woman overcome by a craving is fed until she recovers, since denial could endanger life. An ill person in danger is fed on the advice of medical experts, and if none are present, by his own word until he says he has had enough.

argumentFlow.label: Graduated feeding of forbidden food
argumentFlow.speaker: Mishnah
argumentFlow.text: A baraita: if she craves consecrated meat or pig, one first dips a reed in its juice for her lips; if that does not settle her mind, one gives the gravy; if not, the forbidden food itself, since saving a life overrides every prohibition except idolatry, forbidden relations, and bloodshed.

argumentFlow.label: Source that idolatry overrides life-saving
argumentFlow.speaker: Mishnah
argumentFlow.text: Where do we learn that idolatry is not set aside to save a life? Rabbi Eliezer reads 'with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might' (Deuteronomy 6:5): why state both 'soul' and 'might' if one seems redundant?

argumentFlow.label: Soul and might cover body and property
argumentFlow.speaker: Mishnah
argumentFlow.text: For one who values his body over his property, 'with all your soul' demands he give his life rather than serve idols; for one who values property over body, 'with all your might' demands he give all his possessions. Either way, one forfeits life rather than commit idolatry.

misconceptions.misconception: Saving a life overrides every prohibition in the Torah without exception.
misconceptions.correction: Pikuach nefesh overrides almost everything, but never idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, or bloodshed - one must give his life rather than transgress these three.

visualizableElements.item: Mishna: pregnant woman smells food - feed her unti

quizSeeds.question: Why does one first dip a reed in the juice of forbidden food for a craving pregnant woman?
quizSeeds.answer: To settle her mind with the least possible violation; the forbidden food itself is given only if the lighter steps fail, since saving a life overrides all but three prohibitions.

quizSeeds.question: Which three prohibitions are never set aside even to save a life, and what verse anchors idolatry's place among them?
quizSeeds.answer: Idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, and bloodshed; idolatry is anchored in 'with all your soul' from Deuteronomy 6:5, requiring one to give his life rather than worship idols.

sugyot.finalRuling: A pregnant woman's craving is fed by degrees, up to the forbidden food itself if lesser measures do not settle her, since danger to life overrides every prohibition except idolatry, forbidden relations, and bloodshed; Rabbi Eliezer derives the idolatry exception from Deuteronomy's doubled 'with all your soul' and 'with all your might,' which together require forfeiting life rather than serve idols whether one values his body or his property more.
prerequisiteKnowledge: Background knowledge of pregnant woman context
Understanding of Yom Kippur halachic framework

display.whats: Deriving that one must die rather than commit murder or forbidden relations, from Deuteronomy 22:26
display.hint: Where does the Torah teach that one must give his life rather than commit murder or forbidden relations, and how does the verse comparing rape to murder teach a lesson in both directions - permitting a pursuer to be killed to save a victim, and requiring a would-be murderer to die rather than kill?
display.title: Deriving Martyrdom for Murder and Forbidden Relations from Deuteronomy 22:26

learning.ahaMoment: The verse ostensibly explains rape by comparing it to murder, but the real novelty runs the other way: it uses the settled case (a victim may be saved by killing her attacker) to establish an unstated one (a person must let himself be killed rather than commit murder).
learning.memoryAnchor: Deuteronomy 22:26 compares rape to murder: 'as when a man rises against his fellow and slays him.' Direction one: a betrothed woman may be saved by killing her attacker. Direction two, the real teaching: one must submit to death rather than commit murder - and the same for forbidden relations.
learning.learnerQuestion: Where does Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi derive that one must die rather than commit murder or forbidden relations, and how does the same verse permit killing a pursuer to save a victim?
learning.coreTension: Between reading the verse as merely explaining the law of the betrothed woman by analogy to murder, and recognizing that its real, unstated purpose is to derive a law about murder itself from that comparison.
learning.coreMove: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi derives from Deuteronomy 22:26 - which likens the rape of a betrothed woman to murder - that one must give his life rather than commit murder or forbidden relations. The verse appears to explain the betrothed woman's case using the already-known law of murder (a victim may be saved by killing the attacker), but the Gemara reads the comparison as running in the other, more novel direction as well: just as one may kill a pursuer to save the woman, so one may kill a pursuer to save a murder victim; and just as forbidden relations require submitting to death rather than transgressing, so does murder.

takeaway.text: A single verse comparing rape to murder yields laws in both directions: a pursuer may be killed to save either victim, and one must submit to death rather than commit either murder or forbidden relations - the murder half is the verse's real novelty, not merely borrowed for context.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may read the verse as simply illustrating the betrothed woman's case with a familiar murder analogy; the sugya's point is that the comparison teaches something new about murder itself (die rather than kill), not just about rape.

argumentFlow.label: Source for martyrdom over relations and murder
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Where do we learn one must give his life rather than commit forbidden relations or murder? Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi cites the rape of a betrothed woman: 'as when a man rises against his fellow and slays him, even so is this matter' (Deuteronomy 22:26).

argumentFlow.label: The murder comparison teaches in both directions
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The verse seems to teach about the betrothed woman from the murderer, yet the murderer is the real lesson: just as one may save the betrothed woman by killing her attacker, so one may save a murder victim by killing the pursuer; and just as the murderer must let himself be killed rather than kill, so too in forbidden relations.

misconceptions.misconception: The verse comparing rape to murder is only there to teach the law of the betrothed woman.
misconceptions.correction: The comparison runs both ways: the murderer is actually the lesson, teaching both that a pursuer may be killed and that one must die rather than murder.

visualizableElements.item: Deuteronomy 22:26 (rape compared to murder): a pursuer may be killed to save either victim; one must die rather than commit murder or forbidden relations

quizSeeds.question: What does the Torah's comparison of rape to murder teach in each direction?
quizSeeds.answer: From murder we learn the betrothed woman may be saved by killing her attacker; from the betrothed woman we learn the murderer must let himself be killed rather than transgress.

quizSeeds.question: Why must one surrender his life rather than commit murder?
quizSeeds.answer: The verse equating rape with murder establishes that murder, like the gravest prohibitions, is one a person must die rather than commit.

sugyot.finalRuling: One must submit to death rather than commit murder or forbidden relations, derived by Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi from Deuteronomy 22:26's comparison of rape to murder; the same comparison also permits killing a pursuer to save either victim.

rashiTranslations.he: לא תתני לפני שנה דמשמע שתים ולפני שתים דמשמע ג' שנים אלא אימא מחנכין אותה שנה סמוך לפרק' בחולה ושתים לבריא: תא שמע דתנא
rashiTranslations.en: do not teach 'before one year,' implying two, and 'before two years,' implying three; rather, say: we train her the year close to her maturity for a sick girl, and two years for a healthy one. 'come and hear, for the Tanna

rashiTranslations.he: רבה בר שמואל. שנה או שתים כר' יוחנן ולא תני לפני שנה ולפני שתים: לר' יוחנן ניחא. ומוקי לה שנה לחולה ושתים לבריא:
rashiTranslations.en: Rabba bar Shmuel taught' - 'a year or two,' like Rabbi Yochanan, and does not teach 'before a year' and 'before two years.' 'for Rabbi Yochanan this works well' - and he establishes it as one year for a sick child and two for a healthy one.

rashiTranslations.he: אלא לרב הונא ולרב נחמן קשיא. דהא חינוך לשעות הוא ופחות שבחינוכין לשעות לדידהו ג' שנים הוי דהא אמר רב הונא בתינוקת
rashiTranslations.en: 'but for Rav Huna and Rav Nachman it is difficult' - since training is for hours, and the minimum of trainings-for-hours, in their view, is three years, since Rav Huna said regarding a girl

rashiTranslations.he: חולה שמחנכין אותה בעשירית וברייתא קתני גדול שבחינוכין שתי שנים: מאי חינוך דקתני השלמה. דדבריהם ולדידן נמי השלמה
rashiTranslations.en: who is sick, that we train her in the tenth year, while the baraita teaches the maximum training is two years. 'what is the training that is taught? Completion' - of their rabbinic words, and for us too, completion

rashiTranslations.he: דדבריהם שתים לבריא לפני השלמה דאורייתא אחת לחולה: מתני' עוברה שהריחה. העובר מריח ריח תבשיל והוא מתאוה לו ואם אינה
rashiTranslations.en: of their words: two years for a healthy child before the Torah-law completion, one for a sick child. Mishnah: 'a pregnant woman who smelled' - the fetus smells the smell of a cooked dish and craves it, and if she does not

rashiTranslations.he: אוכלת שניהן מסוכנין: ע"פ בקיאין. אם יאמרו שני רופאים שהוא מסוכן אם אינו אוכל: גמ' כוש. פלך תוחבין לה כוש ברוטב של אותו
rashiTranslations.en: eat, both are endangered. 'according to experts' - if two doctors say it is dangerous if he does not eat. Gemara: 'kush' - a spindle; they insert a kush into the gravy of that

rashiTranslations.he: בשר ומוצצתו: למה נאמר בכל מאודך וכו'. יאמר החביב שבהן וכ"ש שאינו חביב: כי כאשר יקום. בנערה המאורסה כתיב: מה למדנו מרוצח
rashiTranslations.en: meat, and she sucks it. 'why is it stated with all your might, etc.' - let the more beloved of them be stated, and all the more so the less beloved. 'for as when he rises' - is written regarding the betrothed girl. 'what do we learn from a murderer

rashiTranslations.he: לנערה המאורסה. שהוא כמשפט הרוצח כן משפט הדבר הזה: מה נערה המאורסה ניתן רשות. למציל להצילה מבעילת זו בנפשו של בועל
rashiTranslations.en: regarding the betrothed girl' - that just as the law of the murderer, so is the law of this matter. 'just as a betrothed girl, permission was given' - to the rescuer, to save her from this intercourse, at the cost of the life of the one who violates

rashiTranslations.he: זה להורגו עד שלא בא עליה כדכתיב אין מושיע לה (דברים כב) הא יש מושיע יושיענה בכל צידי תשועה: רוצח יהרג ואל יעבור. אם
rashiTranslations.en: her, to kill him before he comes upon her, as it is written 'there is no savior for her' (Deuteronomy 22) - implying that if there is a savior, he should save her by any means of salvation. 'a murderer should be killed rather than transgress' - if

rashiTranslations.he: אמרו לו הרוג חבירך ואם לאו אהרוג אותך יהרג ואל יעבור עבירה זו כדמפרש לקמן: אף נערה המאורסה. אם יאמרו בעול ארוסת חבירך
rashiTranslations.en: they say to him: kill your fellow, and if not, I will kill you - he should be killed rather than transgress this sin, as is explained below. 'so too a betrothed girl' - if they say: violate your fellow's betrothed,

rashiTranslations.he: או תיהרג יהרג ואל יעבור אבל היא אינה מצווה למסור את נפשה דהיא אינה עושה כלום דקרקע עולם בעלמא היא וראיה לדבר אסתר:
rashiTranslations.en: or be killed - she should be killed rather than transgress; but she herself is not commanded to give up her life, since she does nothing, for she is mere inert ground, and the proof for this is Esther.

rashiTranslations.he: ורוצח
rashiTranslations.en: This ('and a murderer') continues on 82b.
